## Findings by module

### 8

- **refined** (ch-002.txt (Chapter I)): On how captives were taken: he believed more were taken by raids between small states and by kidnapping than any other way, and suspected traders' goods tempted chiefs; in his district those sold to the traders from the south-west were prisoners of war or people convicted of kidnapping or adultery. The course's Miles record shows many small dealers; the two accounts differ in scale.
- **contradicted** (ch-002.txt (Chapter V)): Equiano says Barbados held 80,000 enslaved people and needed 1,000 new captives a year, and concludes a life there lasted sixteen years (from Benezet); 80,000 divided by 1,000 is 80, not 16, so the printed figures do not give his conclusion.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt (Chapter I, II)): Equiano says he was kidnapped at about eleven with his sister by two men and a woman who climbed the wall while the adults were in the fields; children watched from trees for kidnappers; the two were separated within days; he travelled six to seven months through several hands to the coast and was sold for 172 shells at a town he calls Tinmah.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt (Chapter I)): In his own society the enslaved did no more work than others, ate apart from the free-born, and some held slaves of their own; one local memory, to be set beside the Songhai and Hausa evidence.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt (Chapters II, III)): Sold at Barbados within about a fortnight in a scramble sale (buyers rush the yard on a drumbeat), shipped on to Virginia, bought by Michael Henry Pascal for 30 or 40 pounds, renamed Gustavus Vassa, reached England in spring 1757 after thirteen weeks, aged near twelve.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt (Chapters V to VII)): Montserrat: sold in 1763 to the Quaker merchant Robert King; paid 40 pounds sterling for his freedom; the manumission of 10/07/1766 records seventy pounds current money of the island.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt (Chapters V, VI, IX)): Legal position of free Black people: no Black person's evidence admitted against a white person, so debts and wages could not be recovered; leaving an island required advertising like a slave; free men such as Joseph Clipson seized and sold; Barbados act fining 15 pounds sterling for killing one's own slave out of wantonness.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt (Chapter XII)): Commissary for the black poor for Sierra Leone from November 1786; stores bought for 750 people but 426 mustered; dismissed 24/03/1787 after complaining of the agent; government paid 50 pounds including 18 wages. The course's over 400 settlers in 1787 is consistent with 426.
- **extended** (ch-002.txt (Chapter XII)): 1789 argument that ending the trade and trading in goods would raise African demand for British manufactures, guessing five pounds a head a year: the legitimate-commerce case was made before the 1807 ban, by an African author.
- **note** (ch-001.txt, ch-002.txt (dedication, Chapter I)): Dedicated to Parliament on 24/03/1789 to stir compassion before the abolition debate; written about 33 years after the kidnapping; he argues his people descend from Abraham through Keturah following Dr Gill, an eighteenth-century theory.
- **note** (ch-002.txt (Chapter XI)): In 1776 he helped Dr Irving buy enslaved Africans at Jamaica for a plantation on the Mosquito Shore, choosing his own countrymen, and managed the work; he later heard the overseer's cruelty drove the enslaved to flee by canoe and drown. He was not only a witness to the system.
